record.original_question: Suppose a basis has Property (A), meaning that moving the largest-magnitude coefficients to new coordinates and changing their signs in the admissible way does not change the norm. Must such a basis be unconditional? Equivalently, is Property (A) by itself strong enough to force greediness, rather than merely 1-almost-greediness?

evidence.quote: To answer this question, F. Albiac and P. Wojtasczyk introduced the Property (A): given x = sum_{n in S} x_n^*(x) x_n with |S| < infinity, we write M(x) := {n in S : |x_n^*(x)| = max_{j in S} |x_j^*(x)|}. Hence, the basis has the Property (A) whenever ||x|| = ||sum_{n in M(x)} epsilon_n x_n^*(x) x_{lambda(n)} + P_{M^c(x)}(x)||.
Theorem 4.19 A basis is 1-almost-greedy if and only if the basis has the Property (A).
Hence, other open question in the field is whether Property (A) implies unconditionality, meaning whether Property (A) is strong enough to imply that the basis is greedy.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Let $X$ be an infinite-dimensional Banach space with a (semi-normalized) Schauder basis $(x_n)_{n=1}^\infty$ and biorthogonal functionals $(x_n^*)_{n=1}^\infty$. For a finitely supported vector $x = \sum_{n \in S} x_n^*(x)\, x_n$ with $|S| < \infty$, define
$$M(x) := \{\, n \in S : |x_n^*(x)| = \max_{j \in S} |x_j^*(x)| \,\}$$
(the set of indices where the coefficient attains the maximum modulus), and let $P_{M^c(x)}(x) := \sum_{n \in S \setminus M(x)} x_n^*(x)\, x_n$.

The basis $(x_n)$ is said to have Property (A) if, for every such $x$, every injection $\lambda : M(x) \to \mathbb{N}$ with $\lambda(M(x)) \cap (S \setminus M(x)) = \emptyset$, and every choice of signs $(\varepsilon_n)_{n \in M(x)} \subset \{-1,+1\}$, one has
$$\Bigl\| \sum_{n \in M(x)} \varepsilon_n\, x_n^*(x)\, x_{\lambda(n)} + P_{M^c(x)}(x) \Bigr\| = \|x\|.$$

Recall that the basis is called unconditional if there is a constant $C$ such that $\|\sum_{n} \varepsilon_n a_n x_n\| \le C \|\sum_n a_n x_n\|$ for all scalars $(a_n)$ and signs $(\varepsilon_n) \in \{-1,+1\}^{\mathbb{N}}$.

Question: Does Property (A) imply that the basis $(x_n)$ is unconditional? Equivalently, must every basis with Property (A) be greedy (rather than merely 1-almost-greedy)?
artifact.status_search_result: A counterexample has been constructed: there exists a Banach space with a Schauder basis satisfying Property (A) which fails to be (1-suppression) unconditional. Hence Property (A) does not imply unconditionality and does not force the basis to be greedy. This appears in "Counterexamples in isometric theory of symmetric and greedy bases" (arXiv:2304.05888).

status_evidence.title: Counterexamples in isometric theory of symmetric and greedy bases
status_evidence.snippet: Provides an example of a Banach space with a basis that satisfies Property (A) but fails to be 1-suppression unconditional.
status_evidence.claim: A basis with Property (A) need not be unconditional, resolving the question in the negative.
